pages.label: Quickstart
pages.title: Build a REST API in Vectrune
pages.description: Create a declarative REST API with URL parameters, JSON validation, and generated Swagger documentation in one Rune file.

sections.title: 1. Install and verify
paragraphs: On macOS or Linux with Homebrew, install the CLI and confirm it is available. Windows binaries and source installation are covered in the developer quickstart.

Releases that bundle offline manuals also install man vectrune for CLI commands and man vectrune-language for language/library details through Homebrew. These manuals match the packaged release; the website may describe newer features.
sections.command:
brew tap davethomas11/homebrew-vectrune
brew install vectrune
vectrune --version

sections.title: 2. Save this as app.rune
paragraphs: The service uses port 3000. Stop another service using that port, or change the port field and the URLs below.

sections.title: 3. Start the service
paragraphs: Run this in the folder containing app.rune. Leave it running and open a second terminal for requests. Stop the server with Ctrl+C when finished.

sections.title: 4. Send requests
paragraphs: The health request returns HTTP 200 and OK. The name route returns HTTP 200 with a serialized object containing name = Ada. The POST returns HTTP 201 with the submitted object. The current REST responder serves these bodies as text, including serialized JSON; do not assume an application/json response header.
sections.command:
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/health
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/greetings/Ada
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/greetings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ada","enthusiastic":true}'

sections.title: 5. Try invalid input
paragraphs: This request omits enthusiastic. The server returns HTTP 400 with Missing field `enthusiastic`.

sections.title: 6. Inspect and test
paragraphs: Open http://127.0.0.1:3000/swagger-ui in a browser. Download api.test.rune beside app.rune to run five request tests without starting a separate server.

pages.label: HTTP routing
pages.title: HTTP routing reference
pages.description: Define Vectrune REST routes, read path parameters, parse JSON request bodies, and return explicit HTTP responses.

sections.title: App and route declarations
paragraphs: Declare @App with type = REST. A route section combines a method and URL, for example @Route/GET /health. Its run series executes statements in order.
The current REST router registers GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. CRUD expands into those methods; PATCH and OPTIONS handlers are not registered by this router.

sections.title: URL parameters
paragraphs: Use braces in the route URL: /greetings/{name}. Parameters enter the execution context as strings, accessible directly as name or through path.params.name.
For numeric comparisons, convert a parameter deliberately with to-number. Do not assume an ID from the URL is already a JSON number.

sections.title: Request bodies
paragraphs: POST and PUT handlers receive the raw request body as body. Run parse-json to replace body with its parsed JSON value, or assign parsed = parse-json body to preserve the raw body.

Each request gets a fresh execution context. Query parameters and general HTTP headers are not automatically exposed by this REST handler. Shared state requires an explicit memory or data-source operation.

sections.title: Responses and execution
paragraphs: respond 201 body returns status 201 and serializes the context variable body. respond 404 "Not found" returns a literal message. A response stops the current request step sequence.

Without an explicit response, the executor can return the last computed result with HTTP 200, falling back to OK when no result is available. A builtin execution error becomes HTTP 500. Use explicit responses and validation for predictable API contracts.

The native REST handler returns a status and a string body. Object serialization does not automatically select application/json; verify the wire response before building clients that depend on response headers.

pages.label: Validation
pages.title: Schema validation reference
pages.description: Validate JSON request bodies with Vectrune schemas, required scalar fields, and explicit HTTP 400 failures.

sections.title: Declare a schema and validate it
paragraphs: @Schema/Greeting declares name = string and enthusiastic = bool. Parse the request body, then call validate body #Greeting before using the input.
The expect = Greeting route metadata connects POST and PUT request bodies to the generated OpenAPI schema. Keep the explicit validate call: expect does not perform runtime validation.

sections.title: Supported validation behavior
items: string accepts a JSON string.
number accepts a JSON number.
bool accepts a JSON boolean; use bool in the Rune schema, not boolean.
Every field declared in the schema is required.
Additional JSON properties are not rejected by this validator.
Nested schemas, optional fields, and array constraints are not implemented by this scalar schema-validation path.

sections.title: Failure responses
paragraphs: Missing fields and type mismatches return HTTP 400 and stop execution. Examples include Missing field `name` and Field `enthusiastic` type mismatch. A missing schema or value returns Validation failed.
Malformed JSON currently produces a builtin error and HTTP 500, rather than a structured HTTP 400 validation response. Account for that behavior when evaluating the API for a client-facing service.
When several fields are invalid, do not depend on which field error is returned first.

sections.title: Exercise valid and invalid requests
paragraphs: The companion test file checks health, a URL parameter, valid JSON, a missing required field, and a scalar type mismatch.

pages.label: OpenAPI
pages.title: OpenAPI and Swagger UI
pages.description: Generate an OpenAPI 3.0 document and interactive Swagger UI from Vectrune REST route and schema declarations.

sections.title: Enable generated documentation
paragraphs: Set swagger = true under @App in a REST application. The server exposes /openapi.json and /swagger-ui.

sections.title: What is generated
items: An OpenAPI 3.0.0 document with title Vectrune API and version 1.0.0. These values are currently fixed by the generator.
Route methods and URL paths, plus the route description when supplied.
Required string path parameters extracted from placeholders such as {name}.
Object schemas from @Schema sections. Declared fields are marked required.
application/json request-body schemas for POST and PUT routes with a known expect schema.

sections.title: Contract limits
paragraphs: The generator includes statically visible respond statuses, HTTP 400 for validate, HTTP 500 for runtime errors, and HTTP 200 when execution can fall through. It does not infer response body shapes from Rune values, so response schemas are strings matching the native REST handler's text/plain wire format.

Generated CRUD routes document their implemented success statuses, validation/not-found statuses where applicable, and runtime errors. Authentication middleware responses are not yet added to the generated contract.
The bundled Swagger UI page loads its JavaScript and stylesheet from unpkg.com. A browser needs access to that CDN to display the UI. The /openapi.json document itself is served locally.

pages.label: GraphQL
pages.title: Build a GraphQL API in Vectrune
pages.description: Define a GraphQL greeting schema, query, and mutation with declarative Rune resolvers and test requests over HTTP.

sections.title: Save as graphql.rune
paragraphs: GraphQL uses its own @App type. Run this example separately from the REST service because both examples use port 3000.

sections.title: Run and query
paragraphs: @Schema/Greeting defines the result object. @GraphQL/Query/Greeting groups fields returning that type; return passes the resolver result back to GraphQL. The greeting query returns a message field.
sections.command:
vectrune graphql.rune
# In a second terminal:
curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ greeting { message } }"}'

sections.title: Call a mutation
paragraphs: @GraphQL/Mutation/Greeting declares greet(message: string). This example returns the supplied message and does not persist it.

sections.title: Explore a stateful example
paragraphs: The repository also includes examples/api/book_graphql.rune, which demonstrates books, authors, memory-backed queries, and mutations. Use that as the next step after this minimal service.

pages.label: WebSockets
pages.title: WebSocket API reference
pages.description: Build a Vectrune WebSocket broadcast endpoint with connection hooks, message handlers, and a browser client.

sections.title: Save as websocket.rune
paragraphs: WebSocket endpoints are mounted by the REST app. This example declares /chat and broadcasts incoming messages to connected clients on that path. Stop other port 3000 examples before starting it.

sections.title: Connect from a browser
paragraphs: Open the developer console on a local HTTP page. This client connects, sends a plain text message when ready, and logs broadcasts. Open a second client to observe fan-out. An HTTPS page may block an insecure ws:// connection.

sections.title: Handlers and builtins
items: on_connect runs after registration of the connection.
on_message handles generic incoming text; body contains the message.
on_disconnect runs when the receive loop ends.
ws.id returns the current connection identifier.
ws.send takes a path, connection identifier, and message.
ws.broadcast takes a path and message, and sends to clients registered on that path.

sections.title: Structured messages
paragraphs: JSON messages with a type property can dispatch to @Event sections. Start with the plain text broadcast example before adding event-specific handlers. Connection and memory registries live in the current process; multiple server processes do not share them automatically.

pages.label: Language map
pages.title: Vectrune language and runtime map
pages.description: Find Vectrune documentation for language syntax, builtins, shared memory, frontend apps, CLI tools, and Pixel game runtimes.

sections.title: Core language and builtins
paragraphs: Rune documents combine @Section paths, key/value data, records, and ordered run steps. The CLI also supports .vect and .vectrune script workflows.

The existing builtin catalog is a starter reference, not a complete inventory. Runtime availability differs between the native CLI, browser emulator, WebAssembly, and frontend JavaScript; check the implementation before assuming a builtin is portable.

sections.title: Shared memory and data
paragraphs: Memory builtins read and write state shared within a running server. Treat it as process-local state rather than durable storage. CSV, JSON, and configured data-source operations provide separate data workflows.
A fresh request context does not isolate shared memory. Decide how application state should behave before serving concurrent users.

sections.title: Web interfaces and deployment
paragraphs: Rune-Web is a frontend mode mounted through @Frontend on a REST app. Static hosting, dynamic AI sites, and Lambda packaging are separate parts of the runtime surface.

In Rune-Web, @Navigator can bind the active route and a separate section fragment. Use fragment = activeSection with mode = path or mode = query to share links such as /#quickstart and restore the selected section on refresh or Back and Forward.

sections.title: Pixel games and Vect Breach
paragraphs: Vect Breach demonstrates the pixel-3d app type with runtime = hybrid. Its entry file imports controls, title scenes, assets, guards, maps, sound, and game logic. @Scene connects those definitions to the camera, things, weapon, HUD, and input controls.

These game declarations form a separate reference area from HTTP APIs. The repository knowledge pages for Pixel 3D, block models, and voxel worlds provide further implementation detail; a complete field-by-field game reference remains future work.

pages.title: Rune DB and Vect Event
pages.label: Database and event streams
pages.description: Run a server-side Rune DB with a Rune-Web frontend, embed providers in existing apps, and commit documents and durable events together.

sections.title: Declare reusable providers
paragraphs: A rune-db datasource stores documents by collection and key. A vect-event datasource shares its store and transaction boundary. Native storage uses redb with MessagePack; browser-local storage uses IndexedDB. This feature requires a compiler built from current source.

sections.title: Run a server-side database with Rune-Web
paragraphs: Recommended: run one server on port 3000. @App type = rune-db owns the native file and @Frontend type = rune-web serves the page. The browser datasource uses mode = remote and endpoint = /, so database requests use the page’s current origin. Both localhost and 127.0.0.1 work, including a --port override, without CORS configuration. Data remains on the server, rather than in IndexedDB.

Save a note, add a view, reload, then load it. Another browser and the CLI read the same server record. Save intentionally replaces this demo note, resets its views to zero and appends note.saved in one atomic batch.

Read new events advances the tab’s cursor through pages of up to 20 events. Replay events starts at zero. The server retains the events; the tab cursor resets on reload. The interface shows event cards, with the raw response under Inspect the response data.
sections.command:
vectrune examples/data/storage/fullstack/single-server.rune

# Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 (or http://localhost:3000), then save a note.
vectrune db get notes hello --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:3000
vectrune events tail notes --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:3000

sections.title: Two listeners from one command
paragraphs: Use --secondary-app to launch independent HTTP apps in the same Vectrune process. Each file keeps its own @App, datasource settings, routes and port. The primary frontend listens on 3000 and the secondary database on 7333. Multiple positional Rune files still merge documents; they do not start separate apps.

Repeat --secondary-app for additional apps. --port and --host override only the primary. Ctrl-C shuts down the group, --watch reloads it, and a bind failure aborts startup before any app starts serving. The option requires Rune app files/directories and cannot be combined with output, input, transform, merge or desktop-target flags.
You can still run app.rune and database.rune in two terminals. Stop the previous version first: the examples share the same native database file.
sections.command:
vectrune examples/data/storage/fullstack/app.rune --secondary-app examples/data/storage/fullstack/database.rune

# The split database endpoint is port 7333:
vectrune db get notes hello --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:7333

sections.title: CORS for the split-server example
paragraphs: Separate ports have different origins. The split database explicitly allows http://127.0.0.1:3000 and http://localhost:3000 using allow_origins, an array of exact HTTP(S) origins. The single-origin allow_origin setting remains supported; use one setting at a time. Wildcard origins are not accepted.

If you change the split frontend port, update this list too. The browser’s origin must match by scheme, hostname and port. The recommended same-server example avoids this cross-origin configuration entirely.

sections.title: The complete Rune-Web frontend
paragraphs: Both hosts import ui.rune and style.rune, so the same note editor, view counter and event history work in either mode. The remote rune-db provider selects the native server; vect-event references that store. Top-level db/events assignments resume after I/O completes, with catch failed reporting errors and re-enabling the controls. The shared styles and all imports are included in the downloadable ZIP.

This unauthenticated example binds to loopback for local development. For external access, configure a server token and HTTPS termination, and supply browser credentials at runtime through __RuneWeb.setDataSourceToken. Use a trusted backend for application authorization; CORS only controls browser origins. Do not embed privileged tokens in downloadable Rune source.

sections.title: Atomic checkout without a server
paragraphs: The local examples use a separate checkout.rdb file. Each checkout run intentionally seeds stock at 10, then atomically decrements it and appends purchase.completed. The expected revision comes from the seed receipt; a concurrent conflicting update rejects the entire batch. Stock and event receipts share a commit position.

Run the replay script twice: the first invocation prints purchases and stores its cursor; the second prints zero events if there are no new purchases. Run checkout again, then replay to resume after the saved position. Each call reads one bounded page. Persist the cursor after processing; a crash before saving can repeat events, so real handlers should tolerate duplicates.
sections.command:
vectrune examples/data/storage/checkout.vect
vectrune examples/data/storage/replay.vect
vectrune examples/data/storage/replay.vect

sections.title: Resume a durable event consumer
paragraphs: local.rune declares main as a rune-db provider and activity as a vect-event view with store = main. The script and its provider file are included in the example ZIP. Run consumers sequentially: this teaching cursor does not coordinate concurrent workers or provide exactly-once delivery.

sections.title: Run an event-only server
paragraphs: This host uses its own file and port 7332, so it can run alongside the database examples. It exposes append, replay and append-only batches; document operations are rejected. after is an exclusive decimal-string cursor. Tail waits for committed events until Ctrl-C.
sections.command:
# Terminal 1:
vectrune examples/data/storage/event-server.rune

# Terminal 2:
vectrune events append orders order.created --value '{"id":"order-1"}' --endpoint http://localhost:7332
vectrune events read orders --after 0 --limit 20 --endpoint http://localhost:7332
vectrune events tail orders --after 0 --endpoint http://localhost:7332

sections.title: Launch a standalone server
paragraphs: Run this server, then use CLI commands from a second terminal. A rune-db host serves document and stream operations; a vect-event host accepts stream operations only. Stop an owning server before directly opening its native file.
sections.command:
vectrune examples/data/storage/db-server.rune

# In another terminal:
vectrune db put notes hello --value '{"count":0}' --endpoint http://localhost:7331
vectrune db increment notes hello --path '["count"]' --by 1 --endpoint http://localhost:7331
vectrune db get notes hello --endpoint http://localhost:7331
vectrune events tail '$changes' --endpoint http://localhost:7331

sections.title: Compose with an existing app
paragraphs: Import the provider declarations into a REST app and call db/events with an operation packet. Writes and their change entries commit atomically. The packet API includes get, get_many, put, delete, increment, bounded prefix scans, append, replay and fixed atomic batches.

sections.title: Keep browser data across reloads
paragraphs: This example saves a note in IndexedDB. Save, reload the page, then load it again. Browser data is local to the origin and does not automatically replicate to the native store. Top-level Rune-Web action I/O resumes after transaction completion; catch handles failures. Use the server-side example above when data must be shared across browsers or devices.

sections.title: Scope and limits
paragraphs: This is a small experimental core: no SQL, joins, consumer groups, automatic replication, branching or commit-block syntax. Names and cursors have defined bounds; values are limited to 1 MiB, packets to 8 MiB and atomic batches to 256 mutations. Revisions and positions are decimal strings.

For full packet forms, retention limitations, authentication and benchmark evidence, read knowledge/runtime/storage.md and examples/data/storage/README.md in the repository. The library db, events, db.request and @DataSource entries identify the supported hosts.
items: get, put, delete and increment address one document by collection and key. Use expected = "0" for create-only, or a returned revision for optimistic concurrency.
scan (CLI alias: query) returns an ordered key-prefix page, not SQL or a property-filter query. Continue with items/next and --after.
append/read operate on ordered streams. Document writes also record $changes in the same transaction. Explicit appends to $changes are rejected.
batch accepts 1–256 put/delete/increment/append operations in one store. A failed operation rolls back all document, revision and event changes.

maintenance.migration: Keep page slugs stable. A future docs subdomain needs a dedicated docs mount or export, updated canonical URLs, sitemap and internal links, asset hosting, and server-side 301/308 redirects from each old /docs/<slug>/ URL to its matching new page. Preserve query strings and test anchors. GitHub Pages alone cannot supply arbitrary HTTP 301 redirects; configure them at the serving proxy/CDN or host.
maintenance.coverage: Supporting API guides; the technical dictionary is maintained in knowledge/reference/library.json and source-derived command inventories.
